notes.title: Units, formulas, resistor code
notes.html:
V = I·RP = V·I = I²·R = V²/RE = P·t (J = W·s; 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J; 1 Wh = 3600 J)Q = I·t (coulombs = amps × seconds)Battery energy: Wh = V × Ah Run time = Wh ÷ WWire: R = ρ·L/A (ρ in Ω·m, A in m²; 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²)Coulomb: F = k·q₁q₂/r², k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ CField: E = F/q (N/C)
QuantityUnitSymbolNamed for
ChargecoulombCCoulomb
CurrentampereAAmpère
VoltagevoltVVolta
ResistanceohmΩOhm
PowerwattWWatt
EnergyjouleJJoule
FrequencyhertzHzHertz

Prefixes: n = 10⁻⁹, µ = 10⁻⁶, m = 10⁻³, k = 10³, M = 10⁶. Convert before you calculate: 15 mA = 0.015 A, 2.2 kΩ = 2200 Ω. Volts ÷ kΩ gives mA.

Significant figures: metric units; give as many significant figures as the least precise number you were given. 12.0 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A.

Resistor color code

0123456789
blackbrownredorangeyellowgreenbluevioletgraywhite

Bands: digit, digit, multiplier (number of zeros), tolerance. Gold ±5%, silver ±10%, brown ±1%. Examples: orange-orange-brown-gold = 330 Ω ±5%; yellow-violet-red-gold = 4.7 kΩ ±5%. Gold and silver as a multiplier (third band) mean ×0.1 and ×0.01. The tolerance band is set apart from the others; read from the end opposite it.

Trap Squaring: P = I²R needs I squared first. Doubling V quadruples P. Doubling a charge doubles F, but doubling the distance cuts F to a quarter.

notes.title: Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)
notes.html:
• Two kinds of charge. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Electrons are the mobile charges in solids. Charge is conserved and quantized: one electron is −1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Field lines point away from + and toward −, in the direction of force on a positive test charge. Field strength E = F/q.
  • Coulomb's Law: F = k·q₁q₂/r². Use meters and coulombs (1 µC = 10⁻⁶ C, 1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C, 1 cm = 0.01 m). The sign only tells you attract or repel.
Worked example. +3.0 µC and +5.0 µC, 0.30 m apart: F = (8.99×10⁹)(3.0×10⁻⁶)(5.0×10⁻⁶)/(0.30)² = 0.1349/0.090 = 1.50 N, repulsive.
Scaling: force ∝ q₁q₂ and ∝ 1/r². Triple r → 1/9. Double one charge and double r → 2/4 = ½.

Charging and polarization

  • Friction (triboelectric): electrons move from one insulator to the other. Glass rubbed with silk: glass loses electrons and becomes positive.
  • Conduction: touching a charged object shares charge, giving the same sign.
  • Induction: a charged rod near (not touching) a neutral conductor moves charge; grounding the far side and removing the ground before the rod leaves a net charge of the opposite sign.
  • Polarization: a neutral insulator (paper, wall) shifts its charges slightly. The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes, so a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.

Static hazards and control

  • Static has voltage but no continuous current. Sparks can ignite fuel vapor or dust. Electrostatic discharge (ESD) can destroy chips.
  • Dry air builds charge; humid air bleeds it away. Grounding, wrist straps, antistatic mats and bags drain charge safely.

notes.title: DC and AC (area iii)
notes.html:
DCAC
DirectionOne wayReverses periodically
SourcesBatteries, solar cells, fuel cells, rectified supplies, USB chargersAlternators and generators, wall outlets
UsesElectronics, LEDs, motors on batteriesPower distribution (transformers easily change voltage)
Typical1.5, 3, 9, 12 V cells120 V / 60 Hz (US), 230 V / 50 Hz (many countries)
  • Period T = 1/f. 60 Hz → 16.7 ms; 50 Hz → 20 ms.
  • Why AC transmission uses very high voltage: P = VI, so the same power at higher V needs less current, and line loss is I²R.
  • Conventional current flows from + to − outside the source. Electrons move the other way. Slides use conventional current.
  • Cells: in series the voltages add (4 × 1.5 V = 6 V). In parallel the voltage stays the same and capacity adds. Dry cell = paste electrolyte (alkaline, zinc-carbon); wet cell = liquid electrolyte (lead-acid). A battery is two different metals plus an electrolyte, so a lemon or potato works (about 0.7 V per lemon with copper and steel, about 1.2 V per Cu-Zn potato cell).
  • Hazards: current through the body does the damage. About 1 mA is felt, 10 to 20 mA can lock muscles, about 100 mA across the chest can cause fibrillation. Voltage drives that current through body resistance; wet skin means lower resistance. A short circuit (near-0 Ω path) gives huge current, heat, fire. Never demonstrate one.
  • Rectifier: diodes turn AC into DC (a single diode = half-wave).

Household AC (2026 list)

  • US outlet: hot (black, ≈120 V RMS to ground), neutral (white, return path, ≈0 V), ground (green or bare, fault path only).
  • RMS is the DC-equivalent heating value: Vrms = Vpeak/√2, so 120 V RMS ≈ 170 V peak.
  • Breaker panel: 15 A and 20 A branch circuits; GFCI at wet locations. Power in a line is P = VI, so I = P/V.

notes.title: Current, voltage, resistance, power, energy (area iv)
notes.html:
• Voltage is the push (J/C), current is the flow (C/s), resistance is the opposition. Water analogy: pressure = voltage, flow = current, narrow pipe = resistance, pump = battery.
  • Resistance of a wire: R = ρL/A. Longer → more R. Thicker → less R (area goes with diameter squared: double the diameter, R ÷ 4). Hotter metal → more R. ρ: silver 1.59, copper 1.68, gold 2.44, aluminum 2.65 (×10⁻⁸ Ω·m). Glass and rubber ≈ 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁶ Ω·m or more.
  • Ohmic parts have a straight-line I–V graph (slope 1/R). Diodes and LEDs do not.
  • Resistor power rating: a ¼ W, 100 Ω resistor can carry at most √(0.25/100) = 50 mA.
  • Energy: E = P·t. Use kW × hours for kWh and cost; use W × seconds for joules. 60 W × 8 h = 0.48 kWh.
  • Efficiency = output ÷ input.
Battery run time. 3.7 V, 2500 mAh → 3.7 × 2.5 = 9.25 Wh. Into a 2.5 W device → 3.7 h. Into a 100 Ω resistor from 9 V with a 500 mAh cell: I = 0.09 A, t = 0.5/0.09 = 5.6 h.
Trap Mixing units. mAh is not Ah. Minutes are not seconds. Check every number has its base unit before multiplying.

notes.title: DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)
notes.html:
Series: same current; voltages add; R = R₁ + R₂ + …
Parallel: same voltage; currents add; 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …; two: R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂); n equal: R/n. The result is below the smallest branch.
Voltage divider: V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂). Current divider (two branches): I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁+R₂); the smaller R takes more current.

Method for any network

  1. Reduce parallel groups and series groups one step at a time until one resistor remains.
  2. I_total = V/R_total.
  3. Expand back: find the voltage across each group, then the current in each resistor (V = IR).
  4. Check: branch currents sum to the node current; drops around the loop sum to the source; Σ resistor power = source power.
Worked example. 18 V, R₁ = 6 Ω in series with R₂ = 12 Ω ∥ R₃ = 12 Ω. Parallel pair = 6 Ω; R_total = 12 Ω; I = 1.5 A. Pair voltage = 1.5 × 6 = 9 V; I₂ = I₃ = 0.75 A. Power: 13.5 W + 6.75 W + 6.75 W = 27 W = 18 × 1.5.

Brightness and power

  • Series bulbs: same current, so larger R gets more power (P = I²R).
  • Parallel bulbs: same voltage, so smaller R gets more power (P = V²/R).
  • Remove one parallel bulb: the others do not change. Remove one series bulb: all go out.
  • Add a resistor in series: total R rises, current falls. Add one in parallel: total R falls, current rises.
  • Load on a divider: a load across R₂ makes R₂ ∥ R_load, so the output drops.
  • Maximum power transfer (bonus): load power peaks when R_load = R_source; then half the power is lost in the source.

Open and short circuits

  • Open: break in the path, I = 0. The break shows the full source voltage across it; every other series part shows 0 V.
  • Short: near-zero resistance path. Current is huge; parts in parallel with the short get ~0 V.
  • A switch that is open has the full battery voltage across its terminals.

Meters

  • Voltmeter: in parallel, very high resistance. Ammeter: in series, very low resistance, never across a source. Resistance: power off, isolate the part.
  • Dial: V with a straight line = DC volts; wavy line = AC (never used here). Leads: red in V/Ω, black in COM. Start on the highest range. Current mode acts like a wire; avoid it, or measure V and R and calculate I.
  • Open circuit on an ohmmeter shows OL or blinking digits.

Schematic symbols to know

Resistor (zigzag or rectangle), battery (long line +, short line −), ground (common 0 V), switch, lamp (circle with X), fuse, LED (diode triangle with two arrows), diode (triangle toward cathode), voltmeter (V in a circle), ammeter (A in a circle). Wires that cross with a dot are connected; without a dot they are not.

Trap Parallel formula: 1/R_total is not R_total. Always finish by checking that the answer is smaller than the smallest branch.

notes.title: Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)
notes.html:
• KCL: current into a node = current out. (Charge is conserved.)
  • KVL: the sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop = 0. (Energy is conserved.)

Two-loop recipe (two unknowns at most)

  1. Label a current in each branch and pick directions. A wrong guess just gives a negative answer.
  2. Write KCL at one node.
  3. Write KVL around two independent loops. A resistor is a drop in the direction of current; a source is a rise when you go through it from − to +.
  4. Solve the pair of equations. Check that power supplied = power dissipated.
Example. E₁ = 19 V and R₁ = 2 Ω on the left, E₂ = 17 V and R₂ = 4 Ω on the right, R₃ = 6 Ω shared. I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 19 = 2I₁ + 6I₃; 17 = 4I₂ + 6I₃. Substitute: 19 = 8I₁ + 6I₂ and 17 = 6I₁ + 10I₂, so I₁ = 2.0 A, I₂ = 0.5 A, I₃ = 2.5 A.

notes.title: Control devices (area vi)
notes.html:
DeviceWhat it does
SPST switchOne pole, one throw: simple on/off
SPDT switchCommon terminal connects to one of two others
DPDT switchTwo poles switched together; cross-wire it to reverse a motor
RelaySmall coil current closes contacts in a separate circuit (NO = open at rest, NC = closed at rest). Add a reverse diode across the coil.
FuseMetal element melts on overcurrent; replace it. In series with the load. Slow-blow tolerates brief surges (motors).
Circuit breakerTrips on overcurrent (heat bends a bimetal strip; a coil handles big shorts); resettable
GFCITrips when hot and neutral currents differ by about 5 mA (leak to ground, e.g. through a person). Protects people.
  • Fuse size: I = P/V, then choose the smallest standard rating at or above I. 90 W at 12 V = 7.5 A → 10 A.
  • Breaker check: I = P/V. A 2400 W load on 120 V draws 20 A and trips a 15 A breaker.
  • Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light). Switches in parallel = OR (either closed).
  • Three-way circuit: two SPDT switches. The commons go to the source (switch 1) and the lamp (switch 2); two traveler wires join the other terminals. Flipping either switch toggles the lamp.

notes.title: Diodes and LEDs (area vii)
notes.html:
• Silicon PN junction: P-type (holes) joined to N-type (electrons) forms a depletion region with a barrier of about 0.7 V. Forward bias (anode positive) narrows it; reverse bias widens it.
  • Forward-biased silicon diode conducts with about 0.7 V drop. Reverse biased: acts like an open switch (tiny leakage) until breakdown.
  • LED: a diode that emits light. Forward drop about 1.8 to 2.2 V red/yellow/green, about 3 V blue/white. Longer lead = anode; flat side = cathode.
  • LED resistor: R = (V_supply − V_f)/I. Round up to a standard value, never down. P = I²R (check the ¼ W rating).
  • Series LEDs: same current; drops add; the supply must exceed the sum. Parallel LEDs: give each its own resistor.
  • Diode drops add in series: two silicon diodes = 1.4 V.
  • Uses: rectifier (AC to DC), reverse-polarity protection (series diode, costs 0.7 V), flyback protection across relay coils, Zener (reverse breakdown for a fixed voltage), photodiode and solar cell (light makes current).
Worked example. 9.0 V, LED 2.1 V, 15 mA max. R = 6.9/0.015 = 460 Ω → use 470 Ω (I = 14.7 mA). A 390 Ω resistor would give 17.7 mA.

notes.title: Digital logic and binary (area viii)
notes.html:
A BANDORNANDNORXORXNOR
0 0001101
0 1011010
1 0011010
1 1110001
  • Precedence: NOT, then AND, then OR. n inputs = 2ⁿ truth-table rows.
  • Gate tricks: AND with 1 passes the input, AND with 0 gives 0. OR with 0 passes, OR with 1 gives 1. XOR with 1 inverts, XOR with 0 passes.
  • De Morgan: (AB)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′B′. Break the bar, flip the operator. So A′B′ = NOR, and NAND of inverted inputs = OR.
  • Identities: A + AB = A, A(A + B) = A, AB + AB′ = A, A + A′B = A + B, A(A′ + B) = AB, AB + AB′ + A′B = A + B.
  • Universal gates: NAND and NOR. With NAND: NOT = 1 gate (tie inputs), AND = 2, OR = 3, NOR = 4, XOR = 4. With NOR: NOT = 1, OR = 2.
  • Truth table to expression: write an AND term for each 1 row (complement the variables that are 0), then OR the terms, then simplify.
  • Multiplexer: n select lines choose among 2ⁿ inputs. 2:1: Y = S′A + SB. A mux with a data input tied to 0 or B can act as AND (select = A, I₀ = 0, I₁ = B).
  • Half adder: Sum = A ⊕ B, Carry = A·B. Full adder: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Carry = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). The sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1. A ripple adder chains full adders.

Binary

  • Place values: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. 101101 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.
  • Decimal to binary: subtract the largest power of 2, repeat. 37 = 32 + 4 + 1 = 100101.
  • Addition: 0+0 = 0, 0+1 = 1, 1+1 = 10 (carry 1), 1+1+1 = 11. Adding two n-bit numbers needs up to n + 1 bits. n bits hold 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
  • Check by converting to decimal: 1101 + 1001 = 13 + 9 = 22 = 10110.

notes.title: Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)
notes.html:
Connectives: ∧ and, ∨ or, → if…then, ~ not, ↔ if and only if. The antecedent is the "if" part. Find the main connective by commas and "both…and", "either…or", "if…then".

RuleForm
Modus ponensP→Q, P ∴ Q
Modus tollensP→Q, ~Q ∴ ~P
Hypothetical syllogismP→Q, Q→R ∴ P→R
Disjunctive syllogismP∨Q, ~P ∴ Q
Conjunctive elimination / additionP∧Q ∴ P; P, Q ∴ P∧Q
Disjunctive additionP ∴ P∨Q
Constructive dilemmaP→Q, R→S, P∨R ∴ Q∨S
Double negation, tautology, commutation~~P = P; P∨P = P; P∨Q = Q∨P
EquivalenceP↔Q = (P→Q)∧(Q→P)
De Morgan~(P∧Q) = ~P∨~Q; ~(P∨Q) = ~P∧~Q
Trap Affirming the consequent (Q, so P) and denying the antecedent (~P, so ~Q) are invalid. In a proof, P in the reason column means premise.

notes.title: Magnetism and induction (adjacent)
notes.html:
Listed on the 2026 Division B page; absent from the 2027 text you were given. Learn the basics in case they return.

  • Poles: like repel, unlike attract. Field lines leave N, enter S, never cross; closer lines = stronger field. Earth’s geographic north is a magnetic south pole. Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted; copper, aluminum and gold are not.
  • Ørsted: current makes a magnetic field. Straight wire (right-hand rule): thumb along conventional current, fingers curl the way the field circles. Coil: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to the N pole.
  • Electromagnet strength: more turns, more current, soft iron core. It switches off with the current.
  • Motor: electrical → mechanical (force on a current in a field, F = BIL; the commutator reverses current each half turn). Generator: mechanical → electrical.
  • Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage. Faster motion, stronger magnet and more turns give more voltage. Lenz: the induced current opposes the change.
  • Transformer (AC only): Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Ideal: Pin = Pout, so stepping voltage down steps current up by the same ratio.
  • Units: tesla (T) for flux density, N/(A·m).
Electromagnet station. Wrap many turns of insulated wire around an iron bolt, connect a battery, test with paper clips. More turns or a second cell picks up more. Keep it brief: the wire and battery heat up.

notes.title: Capacitance (adjacent)
notes.html:
• Two conductors separated by an insulator. C = Q/V (farad; usually µF). Energy E = ½CV² (doubling V gives 4× the energy).
  • Parallel plates: C grows with plate area and with a dielectric, shrinks as the gap grows.
  • Parallel: C adds. Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite of resistors).
  • Once charged in DC, it acts like an open circuit. Electrolytic capacitors are polarized: wrong polarity can fail.
Example. 100 µF at 12 V: Q = 1.2 mC; E = 7.2 mJ.

written: Explain the difference between a fuse and a circuit breaker when current gets too high. Which one protects people from shock?

A fuse has a thin metal element that melts when the current is too high; it opens once and must be replaced. A circuit breaker trips (heat bends a bimetal strip or a coil reacts to a surge) and can be reset. Neither is the shock device: a GFCI protects people by tripping when hot and neutral currents differ by about 5 mA.
Explain why a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.

The balloon’s charge polarizes the wall: opposite charge shifts toward the surface nearest the balloon and like charge shifts away. Coulomb force falls with distance squared, so the nearer opposite charge attracts more strongly than the farther like charge repels, and the net force is attraction.
Describe how to find an unknown resistor Rx using only a voltmeter, a battery and a known resistor.

Connect the known resistor R in series with Rx across the battery. Measure V across R and across Rx. The series current is I = V_R / R. Then Rx = V_x / I = R × V_x / V_R. Power off before rewiring, keep the meter in parallel, and optionally check Rx with the ohm setting with the part isolated.
Design the wiring that makes two identical LEDs equally bright from one 9 V battery. State your resistor value if the LEDs drop 2.0 V and run at 15 mA.

Give each LED its own series resistor of equal value, and connect the two branches in parallel across the battery. R = (9.0 − 2.0)/0.015 = 467 Ω, so use 470 Ω (14.9 mA). Each resistor dissipates I²R ≈ 0.10 W, within a ¼ W rating. Check LED polarity: long lead (anode) toward the resistor and battery positive.
Why does long-distance power transmission use very high AC voltage?

For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current. Heat loss in the line is I²R, so lower current greatly cuts the loss. AC can be stepped up and down with transformers, so it is used for distribution, then stepped down for homes.
Show how to build a NOT gate, an AND gate and an OR gate from NAND gates only, and give the gate counts.

NOT: tie both NAND inputs together (1 gate). AND: NAND followed by a NOT-connected NAND (2 gates). OR: invert each input with a NAND, then NAND the two results (3 gates), because A + B = (A′·B′)′ by De Morgan.
A series loop of a battery, a switch and a lamp is dead. The battery reads 9 V at its terminals. The lamp reads 0 V. The switch reads 9 V. Name the fault and explain how you know.

The switch is open (or has a faulty contact). With no current, the lamp has no drop. Kirchhoff’s voltage law puts the whole source voltage across the one element with the break, which is the switch. Power off, then check the switch contacts and its wires.
A 24 V source feeds R1 = 8 Ω in series with R2 = 24 Ω in parallel with R3 = 12 Ω. Find R_total, the source current, the current in R3 and the power in R1. Show your work.
bench: Mystery resistor (voltage only)
Put a known R in series with Rx across the supply. Measure V across each. R<sub>x</sub> = R<sub>known</sub> × V<sub>x</sub>/V<sub>known</sub>. Report with correct significant figures and units.
Power supplied to a circuit
Voltmeter across the circuit (parallel), ammeter in series. P = V·I. If told to avoid current mode, calculate I from a known resistor’s voltage.
Two equally bright LEDs
Same LED type, each with its own series resistor of the same value, branches in parallel on one battery. Resistor from R = (V − Vf)/I. Check polarity.
USB charger and battery
Read the label for each output level (V and A). P = V·I for each. Battery Wh = V × Ah. Time = Wh ÷ W (divide by efficiency if given).
Logic from a truth table
Write the Boolean expression from the rows with output 1, simplify, then choose gates. For Y = A·B′ use a NOT on B into an AND. Verify every row.
Troubleshoot a faulty circuit

Power off. Look for loose, reversed or missing parts. Power on and measure across each element. The element showing the full source voltage in a series loop is open. A part with 0 V and others too high suggests a short.
Wire a three-way switch
Switch 1 common to the source, switch 2 common to the lamp, travelers join the other terminals, lamp returns to the battery. Test all four switch positions.
Create a target resistance
Choose series (add) and parallel (R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂)) combinations from the parts. Verify with the meter before applying power.
Breadboard and meter basics

Short 5-hole columns are connected on each side of the center gap. Long edge rails run the full length (check for a split in the middle). Red lead V/Ω, black COM, DC volts with the straight line symbol.
Electromagnet (2026 list)
Wind insulated wire around an iron bolt (20+ turns), connect one battery, count paper clips lifted. Double the turns, compare. Disconnect between trials.

questions.q: For which inputs (A,B) does a 2-input XOR gate output 1?

questions.w: Let I₃ = I₁ + I₂. KVL left: 5 = 2I₁ + 1I₃. KVL right: 9 = 3I₂ + 1I₃. Solving gives I₃ = 3 A.
sol: Let I₃ = I₁ + I₂. KVL left: 5 = 2I₁ + 1I₃. KVL right: 9 = 3I₂ + 1I₃. Solving gives I₃ = 3 A.

safety: Eye protection on. De-energize before rewiring. Check polarity first.
Never short a battery. Never put a meter in current mode across a source. Start on the highest range.
Every LED gets a series resistor. Keep water and metal jewelry away.

Two Class III calculators, pencil, color-code and truth-table pages.

hist: Seven names to know: Coulomb, Volta, Ampère, Ohm, Kirchhoff, Boole, Hertz. Each one gave us a law, a unit, or a tool. Learn one clue per person.
Measured the push and pull between charges. Force gets weaker fast as distance grows. His name is the unit of charge: the coulomb (C).
Stacked zinc and copper discs with wet cloth. This "voltaic pile" was the first battery. His name is the unit of voltage: the volt (V).
Showed that wires carrying current push or pull on each other. He linked electricity and magnetism. His name is the unit of current: the ampere (A).
Found that current depends on voltage and resistance.
Two rules for circuits. Current in = current out at a junction. Voltages around a loop add up to zero.
Built an algebra with only TRUE and FALSE (1 and 0). Every logic gate and computer uses his math.
Proved radio waves are real. His name is the unit of frequency: 1 hertz = 1 cycle per second.
Charge = Coulomb. Voltage = Volta. Current = Ampère. Resistance = Ohm. Frequency = Hertz. Logic = Boole. Loops and junctions = Kirchhoff.
static: Positive and negative. Opposites attract. Likes repel. Think of magnets: the same idea.
In solids, only electrons move. Gain electrons and you are negative. Lose electrons and you are positive.
Charge that stays put. It has voltage but no steady current. Rubbing two insulators (balloon and hair) moves electrons from one to the other.
Dry air lets charge pile up. Humid air lets it leak away. That is why winter shocks are common.
Force between two charges. Bigger charges mean a bigger force. More distance means a much smaller force.
Double the distance and the force drops to 1/4. Triple it and the force drops to 1/9. Use meters and coulombs in the formula.
1 µC = 0.000001 C. 1 nC = 0.000000001 C. 1 cm = 0.01 m. Convert BEFORE you plug in numbers.
The push each charge would feel. It points away from + and toward −. Strength is force per charge.
The balloon pushes like charges away inside the wall and pulls opposite charges close. Closer opposite charges win, so it sticks.
Bring a charged rod near (not touching) a metal ball, ground the ball, remove the ground, then remove the rod. The ball keeps the OPPOSITE charge.
dcac: DC flows one way (batteries, solar, USB). AC flips direction again and again (wall outlets).
DC: batteries, solar cells, rectified chargers. AC: generators and power plants.
Transformers can raise AC voltage cheaply. High voltage means low current, so less heat is lost in the wires.
Connect plus to minus and voltages add. Four 1.5 V cells make 6 V.
Connect plus to plus. Voltage stays the same but the battery lasts longer.
Two different metals in a juicy or salty liquid make a cell. Lemon with copper and steel is about 0.7 V. Potato with copper and zinc is about 1.2 V. More cells in series make more voltage.
Frequency is cycles per second. Period is the time of one cycle.
Wall "120 V" is the RMS value. The peak is higher, about 170 V.
Current through the body does the harm. About 10–20 mA can lock muscles. Wet skin lets more current through. Respect every outlet.
Hot carries the voltage. Neutral carries the return current. Ground is only a safety path if something goes wrong.
virpe: Voltage (V) is the push. Current (I) is the flow. Resistance (R) is the squeeze. Power (P) is how fast energy is used.
Know two, find the third. Cover the one you want in the triangle.
V = I × R   I = V / R   R = V / I
Three versions. Pick the one that uses numbers you already have.
Power times time. Use seconds for joules. Use hours with kilowatts for kWh.
Volts times amp-hours gives watt-hours. Divide by watts to get hours of run time.
Wh = V × Ah   hours = Wh ÷ W
m = ÷1000. k = ×1000. µ = ÷1,000,000. Always convert to volts, amps, ohms before calculating.
Longer wire, more resistance. Thicker wire, less. Double the diameter and resistance drops to 1/4.
Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Gray 8, White 9. Bands: digit, digit, zeros, tolerance.
Yellow-violet-red-gold means 4, 7, two zeros: 4700 Ω = 4.7 kΩ, ±5%. Gold = 5%. Silver = 10%.
A resistor can overheat. A 1/4 W, 100 Ω resistor can take at most 50 mA.
Keep as many digits as your least precise number. 12.0 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A.
circ: One path only. Same current everywhere. Resistances add. If one part breaks, everything stops.
Many paths. Same voltage on every branch. Currents add. Resistance goes DOWN: the total is smaller than the smallest branch.
Quick formula for exactly two resistors: product over sum.
Same-size resistors in parallel: divide by how many there are. Three 90 Ω in parallel = 30 Ω.
A 0 Ω path in parallel makes the whole group 0 Ω. All the current takes the short. Dangerous.
Shrink the circuit step by step. Combine each parallel group, then each series group, until one resistor is left.
In series, each resistor gets a share of the voltage. Bigger resistor, bigger share.
In parallel, current splits. The smaller resistor takes more.
Series bulbs: biggest R is brightest (P = I²R). Parallel bulbs: smallest R is brightest (P = V²/R). Unscrew one parallel bulb and the rest stay lit.
OPEN: a break, no current, full voltage across the gap. SHORT: tiny resistance, huge current, heat.
Voltmeter goes in PARALLEL (high resistance). Ammeter goes in SERIES (tiny resistance). Never put an ammeter across a battery.
A load gets the most power when its resistance equals the source resistance. Speakers are matched this way.
Power supplied should equal the power used by all resistors. Branch currents should add up. Drops around a loop should add up.
kirch: Current going into a junction equals current going out. Charge cannot pile up.
5 A and 3 A flow in. One wire takes 2 A out. The other must carry 6 A.
Go around any closed loop. The voltage rises and drops add to zero.
A 12 V battery and three resistors. Two drop 3 V and 5 V. The third drops 4 V.
1) Draw and label a current in each branch. 2) Write one KCL. 3) Write KVL for two loops. 4) Solve the two equations.
Going through a resistor WITH the current is a drop. Going through a battery from − to + is a rise. A negative answer just means the arrow was backward.
Total power from the sources should equal total power in the resistors.
ctrl: SPST: simple on/off. SPDT: switches between two paths. DPST: two on/off switches moved together. DPDT: two SPDT switches moved together.
Pole = how many circuits it controls. Throw = how many positions each pole connects to.
A thin wire that melts when current is too high. One use. Replace it AFTER fixing the problem. It goes in series with the load.
Trips when current is too high. Flip it back to reset. Slightly slower than a fuse. Fix the problem first.
Find current, then pick the next size up.
Trips at about 5 mA of imbalance between hot and neutral. That missing current is leaking through something, maybe a person. Protects PEOPLE.
A small current in a coil closes a switch in a different circuit. Lets a tiny signal control big power. A diode across the coil absorbs the spike.
Switches in series = AND (both must be on). Switches in parallel = OR (either one works).
Two SPDT switches and two traveler wires. Flip either switch and the lamp changes. Commons go to power and to the lamp.
For switch problems, redraw the circuit for each switch setting.
diode: A one-way valve for current. It lets current through in one direction and blocks the other way.
Two silicon types joined together. P-type has extra holes. N-type has extra electrons. Where they meet is the junction.
Adding tiny amounts of another atom. Group 13 atoms (boron) make P-type. Group 15 atoms (antimony) make N-type.
A thin zone at the junction with no free charges. It acts like a wall.
Positive on the P side (anode). The wall shrinks, current flows. Silicon needs about 0.7 V. Germanium needs about 0.3 V.
Positive on the N side. The wall grows and almost no current flows. It acts like an open switch.
Built to conduct backward at a set voltage. Holds a voltage steady.
A diode that gives off light. Color depends on the material. Red needs about 1.8 V. Blue needs about 3 V. Long lead = anode (+).
Always add one. Find the volts the resistor must drop, then divide by the current. Round UP to a standard value.
In series: same current, drops add. In parallel: give EACH one its own resistor so they match.
Rectifier (AC to DC), reverse-polarity protection, relay protection, voltage regulator.
logic: Everything is 1 (on, true) or 0 (off, false). A truth table lists every input and its output.
n inputs give 2ⁿ rows. Three inputs = 8 rows.
AND = 1 only if both are 1. OR = 1 if either is 1. NOT flips it.
NAND is AND then flipped. NOR is OR then flipped. They are "universal": any circuit can be built from just one of them.
XOR = 1 when inputs are different. XNOR = 1 when inputs match.
Do NOT first, then AND, then OR. Like multiply before add.
Break the bar, change the sign. Works both ways.
A + A·B = A.  A·(A + B) = A.  A + A′B = A + B.  A·B + A·B′ = A.
Find rows where output is 1. Write an AND term for each row. OR them together. Then simplify.
NOT = 1 NAND (tie inputs). AND = 2. OR = 3. XOR = 4.
Picks one input using select lines. 2ⁿ inputs need n select lines. 8 inputs need 3.
Adds two bits. Sum = A XOR B. Carry = A AND B.
Adds two bits plus a carry. Sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1.
n bits can hold 0 up to 2ⁿ − 1. 6 bits max out at 63.
hands: Short columns of five holes are connected. The long side rails run the full length. The center gap separates the two halves.
Red lead in the V/Ω jack. Black lead in COM. Pick DC volts (straight line). Start on the highest range.
Touch the probes across the part, power ON. This is parallel.
Power OFF. Take the part out, or lift one leg, so other paths do not fool you.
Put a known resistor in series. Measure both voltages. Same current means voltage ratio equals resistance ratio.
Use identical LEDs. Give each its own resistor of the same value. Put the two branches in parallel on the same battery.
Read volts and amps on the label. Power = V × A. Charge time = battery Wh ÷ charger W (divide again by efficiency if given).
Mix series (add) and parallel (shrink) until you hit the target. Check with the meter BEFORE adding power.
Check the obvious first: power on? battery good? switch on? wire loose? Plugged in is the #1 problem of all time.
Draw the circuit and write the voltage you expect at each part. Measure with power on. Compare.
In a series loop, the part with the FULL battery voltage across it is open. Other parts read 0 V. A part reading 0 V when it should have voltage may be shorted.
Eye protection. Low voltage only. Never short a battery. Never use current mode across a source. Every LED gets a resistor.
sym: Short code for if-then thinking. ∧ means AND. ∨ means OR. → means if-then. ~ means NOT.
If P then Q. P is true. So Q is true.
If P then Q. Q is false. So P is false.
P or Q. Not P. So Q.
Simplification: P∧Q gives P. Addition: P gives P∨Q. Double negation: ~~P = P.
"If P then Q. Q. So P." is WRONG (affirming the consequent). "If P then Q. ~P. So ~Q." is WRONG (denying the antecedent).
mag: Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposites attract. Likes repel. Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets.
They leave north, enter south, and never cross. Closer lines mean a stronger field.
Iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted (ferromagnetic). Copper, aluminum, and gold are not.
A current makes a magnetic field. This was the first link between electricity and magnetism.
Straight wire: thumb along the current, fingers curl with the field. Coil: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to north.
More turns, more current, and an iron core all make it stronger. It turns off when the current stops.
A motor turns electricity into motion. A generator turns motion into electricity. Moving a magnet through a coil makes voltage.
Needs AC. More turns on the secondary means higher voltage.
cap: Two metal plates with an insulator between. It stores energy in an electric field.
How much charge it holds per volt. Unit: farad (F). Most are µF.
Double the voltage and the energy is 4 times bigger.
Parallel: capacitances add. Series: use the reciprocal rule (opposite of resistors).
Once fully charged, it blocks steady current like an open circuit.

glossary: The positive side of a diode. Current enters here.
The negative side of a diode. Current leaves here.
The part doing the work, like a bulb.
A break. No current can flow.
A path with almost no resistance. Huge current.
One path. Parts are in a line.
Many paths. Parts are side by side.
The steady DC value that gives the same heating as the AC.
The voltage direction applied to a diode.
Thin zone at a PN junction with no free charges.
A wire running between two three-way switches.
A gate (NAND or NOR) that can build every other gate.
How far a resistor may be from its labeled value.
Current drawn from + to −. Electrons really move the other way.
stuck: Write down what you KNOW and what you must FIND.
Pick the formula that has those letters. Convert units first.
Plug in, then ask: is the size of my answer sensible?
